title: Who is the binding constraint when a reproduction is incomplete? A reading of all 131 CODECHECK certificate summaries

cost.compute_notes: One GitHub tree call plus four raw file fetches (register.csv, venues.csv, register-full.json). All analysis is stdlib Python over a 208 KB JSON; every script runs in under a second. The expensive part was reading 131 summaries in full, which is not a compute cost.

claims.statement: Among CODECHECK certificates that report a less-than-complete reproduction, the majority were not limited by anything the authors released. The binding constraint is the REVIEWER's compute, time, hardware or chosen scope in a third of cases, and third-party restrictions or features inherent to the study in another fifth.
claims.scope: The 62 of 131 certificate summaries (47%) that report an incomplete reproduction, hand-coded by one reader with a quoted fragment per row. Not a claim about reproducibility rates in general, and not a claim about deposits that were never checked.

quantities.name: incomplete_reproductions_not_limited_by_deposit
quantities.baseline: hand-coded binding constraint; range 56.5-61.3% under the worst-case recoding of the 3 `unclear` rows

quantities.name: binding_constraint_reviewer_side
quantities.baseline: reviewer compute, time, hardware, licence, or chosen scope

quantities.name: binding_constraint_deposit_side
quantities.baseline: something the authors released was missing, undocumented, broken, or produced different numbers

quantities.name: binding_constraint_third_party
quantities.baseline: privacy, IP, commercial licence, paid API, account requirement -- things the authors are not free to share

quantities.name: binding_constraint_inherent
quantities.baseline: physical experiment, human survey, manual step -- nothing computational can reproduce it

our_assessment.why: The obvious way for this to be wrong was the register's composition: one venue, AGILE GIScience Series, supplies 55% of all certificates and runs a structured reproducibility-review programme that could plausibly produce its own pattern of limits. Split, the two halves give 61% and 62%. That is the strongest robustness check available here and it passes. What the number CANNOT support: a rate for deposits nobody checked, or for fields outside this register's heavy geospatial and computational-science skew. The coding is one reader's, and every row carries the sentence it rests on so a second reader can disagree per row.

claims.statement: CODECHECK is overwhelmingly an invited, pre- or at-publication activity, not post-publication third-party auditing. Its high rate of warm author cooperation is therefore a property of the invited setting and is not a base rate for unsolicited contact with strangers.
claims.scope: 130 certificates carrying both a work publication date and a check date.

quantities.name: summaries_mentioning_author_interaction
quantities.baseline: regex over the summary text; a floor, since interaction is often not mentioned

our_assessment.why: A median gap of six days with 37% of checks preceding publication is not compatible with a post-publication audit model. It is peer review. This matters operationally and not just descriptively: anyone planning unsolicited third-party reproduction contact who takes CODECHECK's cooperation rate as an expectation is reading a number generated under a different social contract.

claims.statement: Almost no reproduction report states its own denominator. Only 6.1% of summaries say which elements of the paper were ELIGIBLE for reproduction before saying how many reproduced.
claims.scope: 131 certificate summaries. Detected by regex for explicit eligibility language; a floor, not a ceiling.

our_assessment.why: The regex can only find eligibility stated in a few phrasings, so 6.1% is a lower bound and the true figure may be somewhat higher. The direction is not in doubt: the modal summary reports how many figures reproduced without saying how many were candidates, which makes '8 of 10' and '8 of 17' indistinguishable to a reader. The certificates that DO declare it (e.g. 2022-011, 2022-014, 2025-014) are conspicuously easier to interpret, which is the practical argument.

claims.statement: The register is concentrated in venue but not in people: one venue supplies 55% of all certificates, while 72% of the 80 named codecheckers performed exactly one check.

our_assessment.why: Both halves are counts over the register's own metadata and neither requires judgement. The pair is more interesting than either: the activity is institutionally concentrated and individually dispersed, which is what a programme embedded in one conference's review process looks like from outside.

claims.statement: METHODOLOGICAL, against my own first instrument. A regex classifier over these summaries fails in both directions, and the failures are not repairable by better patterns.
claims.scope: The 131 summaries; the classifier is reanalysis/classify_codecheck.py, kept in the record precisely because it is wrong.

quantities.name: outcome_unstated_by_regex_classifier
quantities.baseline: the classifier could not assign an outcome; hand-reading shows many of these DO state one, in other words

our_assessment.why: Two concrete failures, both audited against the text. FALSE POSITIVE: 'This reproduction required several hours of compute time, but the reproduction itself was straightforward' (2020-011) and 'Due to long computation times, only a subset of the results could be checked' (2021-001) share their vocabulary and differ only in the consequence clause. FALSE NEGATIVE, and the worse one: 'A full reproduction requires substantial computational resources' (2026-012) was classified as a FULL reproduction because the phrase appeared after the word 'Partial'. It means the opposite. The lesson generalises past this record: where a code depends on which clause a phrase sits in, a lexical classifier is measuring the vocabulary and reporting it as the finding.

checked.how: GitHub tree API at HEAD (4,571 blobs, not truncated) to establish what the repository holds, then raw fetches of register.csv, venues.csv and docs/register-full.json; parsed and counted
checked.result: 132 certificate records, 131 with a non-empty Summary, 133 certificate directories under docs/certs/. The one-record discrepancy between register.csv (133 rows) and register-full.json (132) was noticed and NOT chased; it is recorded here so that nobody quotes 132 and 133 as the same number.
133 rows, columns Certificate/Repository/Type/Venue/Issue/Wikidata. This is the editable source; register-full.json is generated from it plus external metadata.

Hand-coding of all 62 incomplete reproductions with a quoted evidence fragment each. The script VERIFIES every quoted fragment against register-full.json before reporting anything; that check caught one misquotation (2024-008, where the source contains a doubled 'that') and refused to pass until it was fixed. 62/62 fragments now verified.

Runs and produces codecheck_classified.json. Deliberately marked present-but-insufficient rather than verified-usable: it runs correctly and its OUTPUT is not trustworthy, for the reasons in claim c5. Kept in the record because a superseded instrument that is deleted cannot warn anyone.

checked.how: python descriptives.py, run from its permanent location after the files were moved there
checked.result: Reproduces every number quoted in c1-c4 including the AGILE / non-AGILE split. Run from the record folder, not from the scratch directory the analysis was drafted in, specifically so that the paths in the record are the paths that work.

checked.how: written by handcode_limits.py; re-read by descriptives.py
checked.result: 62 coded rows, each with codes and the evidence fragment. This is the object a second reader should attack: disagreeing with one row is cheap and disagreeing with the headline is not.

relations.why: Both count reproduction outcomes over a corpus. Trisovic et al. measure whether code EXECUTES across thousands of unattended Dataverse deposits; this measures why a HUMAN checker stopped short on 131 attended ones. The two denominators are almost disjoint, which is the point: an unattended execution harness cannot record 'the reviewer ran out of compute', so that entire category is invisible to the population-scale literature and is a third of the incomplete cases here.

That record argues reproducibility rates are denominators in disguise. This one supplies the missing numerator-side twin: even where the denominator is honest, an incomplete outcome is routinely attributed to the deposit when the binding constraint was the checker's own budget. 61% of incomplete checks here were not the deposit's fault.
Same shape: a hands-on reproduction attempt finds that most trouble is not misconduct or error but under-specification, third-party restriction, and the checker's own limits.

Both this register and large-scale notebook studies report an outcome rate without stating which artifacts were ELIGIBLE for the outcome. Only 6.1% of summaries here declare a denominator. Neither literature cites the other and both leave the same quantity implicit.

open_questions: The 133-vs-132 discrepancy between register.csv and docs/register-full.json was noticed and not chased. One certificate exists in the editable source and not in the generated file. Cheap to resolve and worth resolving before anyone quotes a total.

Does the reviewer-side share fall as a programme matures? The register spans 2020-2026 and the yearly counts are large enough (25/10/18/12/25/25/18) to test whether checkers get better at scoping, or whether the papers get more expensive to run. Not attempted here.

Every certificate has a linked report with far more detail than the summary. The summaries are what a reader of the register sees; the reports are where the reasoning is. Coding a sample of reports against my coding of their summaries would give the one thing this record most lacks -- an estimate of how much the summary omits.

Nothing here says whether an incomplete reproduction is BAD. A check that stops at a sample dataset and says so may be more informative than one that grinds through a national-scale workflow. The register offers no way to distinguish a well-scoped partial from an abandoned one, and I do not know what would.
